newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: Mood turns ugly as punters stumble on Dhaka kerb.
newsitem.headline: Mood turns ugly as punters stumble on Dhaka kerb.

text.p: Small investors trading outside the Dhaka Stock Exchange turned on journalists and cameramen on Monday as they saw mounting losses on their transactions.

"Catch them and kill them," shouted traders as they chased journalists away from the the open-air market where workers, housewives and students, some carrying sackfuls of share certificates, engaged in raucous trade.
"I just narrowly escaped. I faced a barrage of rocks and even sandals. They hurled everything at us," said a press photographer.

Hundreds of police were posted on the streets and avenues bordering the exchange in anticipation of trouble after the DSE all-shares index fell by more than six percent on Sunday, a working day in Moslem Bangladesh.
The index continued to fall in early trading on Monday, adding to the woes of the small investors.

The "kerb" market has crumbled over the past few days after the Securities and Exchange Commission, the market watchdog, circulated a list of 24 losing companies and warned investors against buying the shares.
Small investors were left with millions of highly overvalued shares on their hands after the commission's warning was broadcast on state television last week and sent the shares tumbling.
Trader desperate to sell advertised their shares by shouting and waving signs on Monday.
"I have incurred so many losses that I will almost run out of business," said investor Mynul Huq, who had put 400,000 taka ($10,000) into the exchange over the past two months.
Many of the investors blamed the media.
"The newspapers are to largely blame for our bad luck," one investor said.
"Newspapers printed speculative and baseless stories that triggered panic selling...and led to an unexpected downtrend in a strong market," said investor Shoheil Ahmed.
The DSE all-share price index closed 121 points, or 6.25 percent, down at 1,813.44 on Sunday. This followed a drop of 4.44 percent on Saturday.

The index dropped after the DSE imposed a limit on share price movements to stop wild trading and the quotation of speculative prices. The new rule, which took effect on Saturday, limits share price movements to 10 percent of the previous day's rate.
